messages.subject: multiplier for suitable/potential habitat?
parts:
Hello,=20

I feel that my question may have a straightforward answer, so I'm includi=
ng minimal back-story here.=20
I've conducted 212 point count surveys for marsh birds at the landscape s=
cale, replicated 3 times each. Survey points are reached by, and conduct=
ed from a boat. Detections have been truncated to a 200 meter buffer surr=
ounding each point to avoid overlap in surveyed areas. The issue here is =
concerning "suitable habitat". As I understand, DISTANCE estimates densi=
ties within the user defined area (200 meter truncation in this case - bi=
rds/hectare). However, since all of these surveys are conducted along a c=
hannel (of varying widths at each point), a portion of the area is not po=
tential habitat.=20

I'm wondering if including the area that IS potential habitat as a point =
transect attribute would be a way to incorporate this into the density es=
timate? Or, if I could simply adjust the estimate to reflect potential ar=
ea after the analysis? These estimates will be used as the response vari=
able for habitat modeling. This is more of a methods question and possibl=
y out of the realm of this forum, but I could also simply use the "emerge=
nt marsh within 200m" as a predictor variable in the analysis. I can't w=
rap my head around the best thing to do in this case. Certainly, there ar=
e more elegant ways to do this, but I'm working with the best I have for =
the time being.=20

Thanks in advance for your comments and time.=20
Sincerely,
Ali Leggett

messages.author: 4cacbe3a86a908bf
messages.subject: Re: multiplier for suitable/potential habitat?
parts:
Hi Ali, list,

Some unfinished thoughts, but your question really begs for (at least!)=20
2 answers:

1. if you are covering suitable and unsuitable habitat with areas As and=20
Au respectively, and if you assume that density is 0 in unsuitable=20
habitat and Ds in the suitable habitat, then the overall density happens=20
to be D=3D(Ds*As+0*Au)/(As+Au). All else being OK, if you ignore the=20
different densities, D is what you estimate from your distance sampling=20
analysis, so if you want to get density in the suitable area you have to=20
do some simple maths to get it back. The above formula allows you to get=20
Ds from D. But this actually assumes that points are located at random=20
with respect to suitable and unsuitable habitat, which does not seem to=20
be your case, which leads to...

2. the survey you describe is non-standard because the suitable habitat=20
is actually decreasing as a function of distance to the point (because=20
the point is always placed in suitable habitat, right?), so effectively=20
not only detectability is decreasing as a function of distance, but=20
availability of animals decreases as a function of distance. It becomes=20
less clear cut what happens then. Section 6.7 in the introduction to=20
distance sampling book says that if the model you use for the detection=20
function is flexible enough (but that is of course rather vague) then=20
you are modelling the joint effect of detectability and availability=20
(see eq. 6.41 on page 215), and you might still be able to estimate=20
density AT THE POINT. But if that is the case then actually you are=20
estimating Ds directly rather than D, so no correction would be required=20
to estimate Ds.

The problem here is that now the estimated detection function is not=20
simply reflecting detectability, and hence correcting the observed=20
counts to feed into as responses into a model becomes harder to do. If=20
you have the available areas mapped in a GIS you can have some "fun"=20
estimating the true detection function given explicit modelling of e(x)=20
in equation 6.44, and that gets you a step closer to what you need.

hope this helps.

Tiago
